column1: # tests/coverage-floor.tsv - Q11: coverage may not go down.
# One row per file the host tier builds: the line-coverage percentage
# below which `make coverage-check` fails. Raised by hand, with the
# commit that raised it, exactly like tests/budgets.tsv - and lowered by
# hand too, because deleting a test can be the right call and should have
# to be said out loud rather than happening quietly.
# Q8 deliberately set no coverage *target*, and that still stands: the
# absolute number is whatever the tests honestly reach. This constrains
# A caveat worth carrying next to these numbers: line coverage is the
# weaker of the two instruments here. `net/ethernet.c` sat at 100% lines
# with a **0%** mutation score until Q12 looked - every line ran and
# nothing asserted what any of them did. Read this file next to
# M101: the names here are repo-relative paths, and they used to be
# relative to kernel/ instead. llvm-cov prints each file with the longest
# common prefix of everything on its command line removed, so adding the
# first user-space source to the report shortened nothing and lengthened
# every kernel name. Every floor in this file stopped matching, and the
# ratchet reported ten "new" files and "nothing fell" - which is a
# ratchet that has quietly stopped ratcheting. tools/coverage-ratchet.py
# now fails when a name in this file is absent from the report, so the
# next time that happens it is an error rather than a silence.
# M100: the floors are the MEASURED number now, not a round number under
# it, and every file in the report has one.
# Both changes are the same repair. Rounding 83.82 down to 83 meant the
# ratchet printed "raised ... raise it, and say so" for seven files on
# every run, forever, and eight more files had no row at all and printed
# "new" on every run. Fifteen lines of advice nobody was going to act on,
# on every single run - and underneath them, two floors that had actually
# FALLEN and had been falling since M98. The noise is what hid them.
# So: exact values, and tools/coverage-ratchet.py now fails on a file
# with no row rather than printing one more line. The report should be
# silent when nothing changed, because that is the only state in which

Its own comment had warned about exactly that, three lines above the table it needed a row in. 100% now: the switch table in tests/test_fwcfg.c is derived from one array, every switch is asked on every case, and each is asked twice.

M100: exact rather than 97. M101: the profile report's symbol resolver, and the first user-space file in this tier. Four hand-run mutations against its tests were all caught, which is the number that matters more than this one.

Every function takes the time as an argument, which is why a test can ask what this file does at 1099.999 ms - see its header for why that decision was made against tcp.c's precedent rather than in ignorance of it.

M183: 98.67 -> 97.11, and LOWERED to a MEASUREMENT rather than to a preference. This is the first time this ratchet has run since M157, which put libintl.c in TEST_USER_SRCS while COV_CFLAGS had no way to reach <libintl.h> - so `make coverage` stopped compiling and every floor here has been unchecked for twenty-six milestones. M171 grew the memfd table into one that doubles; the lines that arrived with it are its growth-failure path, which needs a kmalloc that fails. Measured on M182 with the build repaired and nothing else changed: 97.11. The number is the truth about the tree rather than a target anybody aimed at, and the condition for raising it again is a test that drives that path. M120: first floor. Shared memory a descriptor names. The three uncovered lines are the heap-failure path in memfd_truncate's array growth. Mutation score 89.3% - 82.1% on the first run, and two of the five survivors were assignments in memfd_init that nothing could notice, which is how that function came to do one thing instead of six.

The boot-report decoder is pure: bytes in, key events out, so 100% is what it should be.

M127: first floor, same M107 gap. This is the one path QEMU cannot reach at all - its namespace has 512-byte blocks, so a 4Kn drive's read-modify-write split is dead code on this machine and would first execute on somebody's real filesystem. 100% here is not a nicety.
